from manim import *

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

class Section1Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = [
            "A line has length, a plane has area.",
            "Can one continuous line fill a 2D square?",
            "Intuition says no, but math says yes.",
            "We bridge dimensions with space-filling curves."
        ]
        self.setup_layout("The Dimensional Paradox", lecture_lines)

        # Assets/Objects
        line_segment = Line(start=LEFT, end=RIGHT, color=BLUE).scale(0.5)
        square = Square(side_length=2, color=YELLOW)
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.play(FadeIn(self.lecture[0]))
        self.place_at_grid(line_segment, 'B2')
        self.place_at_grid(square, 'B5')
        self.play(Create(line_segment), Create(square))
        self.lecture[0].set_color(BLUE)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.play(FadeIn(self.lecture[1]))
        self.play(line_segment.animate.move_to(self.grid['E3']), run_time=1)
        self.lecture[1].set_color(YELLOW)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.play(FadeIn(self.lecture[2]))
        self.play(Indicate(square))
        self.lecture[2].set_color(GREEN)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 4 ===
        self.play(FadeIn(self.lecture[3]))
        curve = VGroup(*[Dot(self.grid[f"{r}{c}"], radius=0.05, color=RED) for r in "BCDE" for c in "345"])
        self.play(FadeIn(curve))
        self.lecture[3].set_color(RED)
        
        self.wait(2)

class Section2Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = [
            "Start with a simple grid of squares.",
            "Trace a path through each subdivision.",
            "Recursion creates infinite complexity."
        ]
        self.setup_layout("The Peano Curve Construction", lecture_lines)
        
        # Initial state setup
        grid = VGroup(*[Square(side_length=0.8, color=BLUE_D) for _ in range(9)]).arrange_in_grid(3, 3)
        self.place_in_area(grid, "B2", "D4", scale_factor=1.0)
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.play(Create(grid), self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(BLUE))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Simple trace path
        path = VMobject(color=YELLOW)
        path.set_points_smoothly([grid[0].get_center(), grid[1].get_center(), grid[2].get_center(),
                                  grid[5].get_center(), grid[4].get_center(), grid[3].get_center(),
                                  grid[6].get_center(), grid[7].get_center(), grid[8].get_center()])
        self.play(Create(path), self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(YELLOW))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # Visualize recursion concept: sub-dividing
        new_grid = VGroup(*[Square(side_length=0.25, color=BLUE_E) for _ in range(81)]).arrange_in_grid(9, 9)
        self.place_in_area(new_grid, "B2", "D4", scale_factor=1.0)
        self.play(FadeOut(grid), FadeOut(path), FadeIn(new_grid), self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(RED))
        self.wait(2)

class Section3Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = ["Hilbert curves are a more efficient alternative.", "The L-shape logic preserves spatial locality.", "Points close on line remain close in space."]
        self.setup_layout("The Hilbert Curve: Efficiency in Recursion", lecture_lines)
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(BLUE))
        # Simple visual representing "efficiency": a growing curve
        hilbert_base = VGroup(
            Line(UP, ORIGIN), Line(ORIGIN, RIGHT), Line(RIGHT, UP+RIGHT)
        ).set_color(YELLOW)
        self.place_in_area(hilbert_base, 'A1', 'C3', scale_factor=0.5)
        self.play(Create(hilbert_base))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(GREEN))
        # Visualization for L-shape rotation (mimicking [Asset: Hilbert_L_Shape_Evolution])
        l_shape = VGroup(
            Line(UP, ORIGIN), Line(ORIGIN, RIGHT)
        ).set_color(RED)
        self.place_at_grid(l_shape, 'D4', scale_factor=1.0)
        self.play(Create(l_shape))
        self.play(l_shape.animate.rotate(PI/2, about_point=self.grid['D4']))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(ORANGE))
        # Points to show locality
        p1 = Dot(color=PURPLE)
        p2 = Dot(color=PURPLE)
        self.place_at_grid(p1, 'E1')
        self.place_at_grid(p2, 'E2')
        self.play(Create(p1), Create(p2))
        self.play(Flash(p1), Flash(p2))

        self.wait(2)

    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = ["Curves optimize database indexing and storage.", 
                         "They also enhance image processing tasks.", 
                         "Locality helps computers access data faster."]
        self.setup_layout("Real-World Applications", lecture_lines)

        self.place_at_grid(dots, 'E3', scale_factor=1.5)
        self.add(dots)
        
        # Animate sorting movement (simplified path)
        path = VMobject().set_points_smoothly([dots[i].get_center() for i in range(len(dots))])

        self.add(path)
        self.play(Create(path))
        self.play(FadeIn(dots))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(colors[2]))
        speed_arrow = Arrow(start=ORIGIN, end=RIGHT*1, color=ORANGE)
        self.place_at_grid(speed_arrow, 'C5')
        self.add(speed_arrow)
        self.play(Indicate(speed_arrow))
        self.wait(1)

class Section5Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = ["Space-filling curves flatten higher dimensions.", "Nature uses these to maximize surface area.", "Fractals pack complexity into minimal volumes."]
        self.setup_layout("Conclusion and Intuitive Summary", lecture_lines)
        
        # Animations
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(BLUE))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(GREEN))
        
        # Load asset without path joining complexity
        # The environment handles the assets_dir, so filename should suffice.
        try:
            nature_image = ImageMobject("Conclusion_Nature_Overlay")
            self.place_in_area(nature_image, 'A1', 'F6', scale_factor=0.5)
            self.play(FadeIn(nature_image))
            self.wait(1)
        except Exception:
            pass # Graceful failure if asset missing

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(YELLOW))
        self.wait(2)

sections.title: The Dimensional Paradox (0:00-0:45)
sections.content: Introduce the prerequisite concept: A 1D line has length, and a 2D plane has area. Pose the question: Can a continuous line pass through every single point in a 2D square? Challenge the intuition that a line has 'zero area'.
sections.example: Visualize a thin thread moving across a square grid; show how it can never fill the 'gaps' until it infinitely twists.

sections.title: The Peano Curve Construction (0:45-2:00)
sections.content: Explain the recursive algorithm. Start with a square grid (1x1), subdivide into 9 smaller squares, and trace a path through them. Show that as the iteration count 'n' approaches infinity, the path effectively covers all points.
sections.example: An animation of a 'snake-like' path subdividing into smaller segments, demonstrating how complexity increases with each iteration step.

sections.title: The Hilbert Curve: Efficiency in Recursion (2:00-3:15)
sections.content: Introduce the Hilbert curve as a more popular alternative to Peano. Explain the 'L-shape' rotation logic. Emphasize that it is continuous, surjective, and maintains locality (points close together on the line are close in the 2D space).
sections.example: A visual comparison: Hilbert curve vs. a random scribble, showing how the Hilbert curve maps a 1D sequence to a 2D layout without 'jumping' across distant areas.

sections.title: Real-World Applications (3:15-4:30)
sections.content: Explain why this matters: Database indexing (mapping 2D geographical data to 1D disk storage), image processing, and fractal antenna design. Explain that 'locality' helps computers read data faster.
sections.example: A 'Pixel-sorting' robot character moving along a Hilbert path to organize scattered colored dots into a coherent image efficiently.

sections.title: Conclusion and Intuitive Summary (4:30-5:00)
sections.content: Summarize the key takeaway: Space-filling curves are infinite limits of simple patterns that allow us to 'flatten' dimensions. Encouraging students to see fractals as nature's way of maximizing surface area.
sections.example: A final graphic showing a human lung or a fern leaf, highlighting how nature uses space-filling principles to pack maximum surface area into minimal volume.
